paragraphs: A beluga whale was seen in Donegal Bay on 17 October. Belugas are white whales. They usually live in the cold Arctic sea. It was a rare visit.

A beluga whale has been seen in Donegal Bay, far from its usual home. Belugas are white whales that normally live in the cold waters of the Arctic.

On 17 October, Sebastian Szumlański filmed the whale with a drone at Fintra. He shared the video with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG). It is only the second beluga sighting the group has officially confirmed. The first was off Co Antrim in 2015.

Pádraig Whooley, who records sightings for the group, said the whale is an adult about four metres long. He said it is a beautiful, bright white colour. Many belugas have marks from attacks by polar bears.

Whooley said more Arctic animals, such as walruses, narwhals and bowhead whales, are now turning up in Irish waters. He believes warmer seas are changing where these animals live, and some have "nowhere left to go".
Storm Austen made it harder to watch the whale from the shore. Whooley asked the public to report any whales or dolphins they see.
A beluga whale has been spotted in Donegal Bay, the latest in a growing number of Arctic species to appear in Irish waters.

Sebastian Szumlański captured drone footage of the animal at Fintra on 17 October and shared it with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG). It is only the group's second validated beluga record, after one off Dunseverick, Co Antrim, in 2015, although a handful of earlier sightings date back to 1948.

Pádraig Whooley, the IWDG's sightings officer, said the whale was an adult measuring roughly four to four and a half metres and was a brilliant white. He noted that many belugas carry scars from polar bear attacks.

Whooley described a clear trend of Arctic visitors, including bowhead whales, walruses and narwhals, being recorded more often around Ireland. He linked this to warming oceans, which are disrupting the animals' habitat and leaving them with "nowhere left to go".
The sighting coincided with Storm Austen, which made observation from the shore difficult. The IWDG is urging members of the public to report any whale or dolphin sightings.
A beluga whale has surfaced in Donegal Bay, the latest in a string of Arctic species to stray into Irish waters in recent years.

Sebastian Szumlański filmed the animal by drone at Fintra on 17 October and passed the footage to the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG). Remarkably, it constitutes only the group's second verified beluga record, the first having been logged off Dunseverick, Co Antrim, in 2015, although sporadic sightings stretch back as far as 1948.

Pádraig Whooley, the IWDG's sightings officer, described the creature as a mature adult of some four to four and a half metres, with a dazzling white hue. Many belugas, he observed, bear the scars of encounters with polar bears.

Whooley pointed to an unmistakable pattern of Arctic visitors, among them bowhead whales, walruses and narwhals, turning up with increasing frequency. He attributes this to warming seas eroding their habitat, leaving such animals with "nowhere left to go".
The sighting coincided with Storm Austen, which hampered efforts to observe the whale from land. The IWDG has appealed to the public to report any cetacean sightings.
A beluga whale has been observed in Donegal Bay, constituting the most recent example of a broader phenomenon whereby Arctic species are increasingly recorded in Irish waters.

On 17 October, Sebastian Szumlański obtained drone footage of the animal at Fintra and subsequently submitted it to the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG). This represents only the organisation's second validated beluga record, the first having occurred off Dunseverick, Co Antrim, in 2015, although isolated sightings have been documented since 1948.

According to Pádraig Whooley, the IWDG's sightings officer, the specimen is a mature adult measuring approximately four to four and a half metres, with exceptionally white colouring. He further noted that many belugas exhibit scarring attributable to polar bear attacks.

Whooley identified a discernible trend in which Arctic species, including bowhead whales, walruses and narwhals, are appearing with greater frequency. He attributes this primarily to rising ocean temperatures, which are degrading their natural habitat and consequently leaving these animals with "nowhere left to go".
The sighting coincided with Storm Austen, which substantially impeded observation from the shore. The IWDG has therefore encouraged the public to report any whale or dolphin sightings.
